details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: Is there a maximum throughput rate or resource-consumption ceiling (e.g., machine utilisation ≤ 90 %, labour intensity ≤ standard-pace × 1.1) beyond which you would not want the optimiser to push, even when fatigue and noise hard constraints are technically satisfied? Without a cap, a 'maximise' objective on an unbounded KPI can legally drive the system into unsustainable, near-limit operating conditions.
flags.resolution: Cap machine utilisation at 85 % and labour pace multiplier at 1.05× standard rate; resource_efficiency is therefore optimised only within this feasible envelope.

flags.question: What is the planned shift duration in hours (e.g., 8 h, 10 h, 12 h), and does that figure include scheduled rest breaks or only net productive time? Shift length directly determines fatigue accumulation rates and whether the ≤ 0.4 fatigue ceiling is achievable at any positive efficiency level.
flags.resolution: Assume an 8-hour shift with two 15-minute rest breaks and one 30-minute meal break, yielding 7 hours of net productive time; all fatigue-model parameters are scaled to this horizon.

flags.question: How should labour-hours, machine-hours, energy, and raw-material inputs be combined into a single resource-efficiency denominator — equal weight, internal cost rates, or energy-primary weighting? Different schemes can make opposite decisions optimal (e.g., substituting cheap energy for expensive labour versus conserving energy at the cost of overtime).
flags.resolution: Apply cost-based weighting using the plant's standard internal cost rates for each resource category; rates are sourced from the ERP system at shift start.

flags.question: Should the optimiser treat the hard ceiling of 0.4 as an ordinary operating point (running fatigue at 0.38–0.40 when efficiency demands it), or should it pursue a lower soft target (e.g., ≤ 0.30) and only allow up to 0.40 under unavoidable peak load? Your stated intent is to keep fatigue 'low', which suggests the ceiling is a safety backstop rather than a design target.
flags.resolution: Introduce a soft fatigue target of ≤ 0.30 as a secondary KPI objective; the hard constraint of ≤ 0.40 remains inviolable, and any schedule that breaches 0.30 is penalised in the objective function.

flags.question: When resource efficiency and human wellbeing conflict at the margin — for example, the highest-efficiency schedule holds fatigue at 0.39 and noise at 79 dB, just inside both hard constraints — should the optimiser accept that schedule, or should it sacrifice some efficiency to drive fatigue and noise meaningfully below their ceilings? The contract lists HumanWellbeing first in priority_order but gives no penalty for operating near (rather than at) the limits.
flags.resolution: The hard constraints on fatigue (≤ 0.40) and noise (≤ 80 dB) are enforced as inviolable; within the feasible space the optimiser maximises resource_efficiency without applying a further penalty for proximity to the constraint boundary, unless the soft fatigue target ambiguity (item 4 above) is resolved otherwise.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The contract schedule S1 was written assuming a baseline demand of 52.0 UPH. With actual demand at 59.8 UPH (+15%), the total unit target for Phase 2 is proportionally larger than the schedule's production envelope. Current throughput stands at 32.7 UPH — only ~54.7% of the elevated demand rate — meaning the system is accumulating a production deficit every hour. This deficit directly erodes the time buffer embedded in the DeadlineGap constraint: the schedule assumed the buffer was sized against 52.0 UPH, but the 7.8 UPH demand overshoot generates additional backlog units that cannot be absorbed within the remaining phase window at the current output rate. The result is that the deadline gap margin (0.453) is insufficient to clear the accumulated shortfall before the phase deadline, constituting a constraint breach.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Escalate immediately to shift supervisor and schedule controller. Evaluate feasibility of temporarily increasing robot cycle rate to narrow the throughput-to-demand gap, while monitoring noise_db (currently 78.6 dB, check ceiling) and energy_kwh (359.0, check capacity). If throughput cannot be raised sufficiently, initiate demand-side triage: prioritize highest-value SKUs and defer lower-priority units to Phase 3 or a rescheduled run. Trigger a contract re-baseline to update demand_base_uph to 59.8 and recompute DeadlineGap slack for remaining phases.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: Fatigue index is the primary violation (0.5912 vs 0.4 limit). Fatigue scales approximately proportionally with human cycle rate. Applying the proportional reduction: 1.18 × (0.4 / 0.5912) ≈ 0.799, rounded to 0.80. This is the most direct and isolated lever for the fatigue constraint — robot adjustments do not affect it.

R1 operates at the highest speed fraction (0.90) and is therefore the dominant contributor to mechanical noise through motor harmonics and kinematic vibration. A targeted reduction of 0.08 on the fastest robot yields the greatest noise-per-unit-adjustment ratio. Noise in dB from a rotating machine scales with roughly 20·log10(speed), so reducing R1 from 0.90 to 0.82 (a 9% speed drop) yields approximately 1.5–2 dB attenuation on the loudest source.

R2 at 0.88 is the secondary noise source. After R1's reduction above, residual noise is still likely 1–2 dB above the 80 dB ceiling. Reducing R2 by 0.08 provides the complementary attenuation needed to close the gap. Both robot reductions together lower the combined acoustic power sufficiently to meet the 80 dB hard constraint. Note: these speed reductions will modestly decrease throughput from 45.6 UPH, but the human_cycle_rate reduction also relaxes the human bottleneck, partially offsetting the robot-side loss.

details.conflict: A 15.0% demand surge has rendered the proposed production schedule infeasible under current human-centric constraints. Two violations were detected: (1) FatigueIndex reached 0.5912, exceeding the worker safety limit of 0.40 by a margin of 0.1912 — representing a 47.8% overage; (2) Noise exposure reached 82.9 dB, exceeding the occupational health ceiling of 80.0 dB by 2.9 dB. The CBPA governance layer has automatically rejected this schedule and escalated for human review. No autonomous relaxation of these constraints has been applied. Immediate action is required to either reduce demand, augment capacity, or obtain an authorized temporary waiver with documented worker protection measures.
options: Option 1 (Recommended) — Demand Deferral: Preserve All Constraints
Option 2 (Conditional) — Shift Augmentation with Minimum Necessary Relaxation
Option 3 (Last Resort) — Temporary Emergency Override with Full Demand Fulfillment

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with FatigueIndex at 100% violation probability signals complete infeasibility that cannot be addressed by MICRO parameter tweaks. Increasing robot speeds to absorb the +15% demand surge would directly worsen fatigue—a fundamental policy-level contradiction, not a calibration error. However, prior learning from 1 similar situation shows that S3 was accepted while S2 was rejected, indicating a policy family switch is the proven lever for this disturbance pattern. MACRO full replanning is not yet warranted because an analogous scenario was resolved at the MESO tier.
details.reasoning_key_insight: The FatigueIndex and demand surge are structurally at odds under the current policy: any speed increase to meet demand amplifies fatigue violations. A policy family switch to S3 (the accepted precedent) reframes the scheduling logic—potentially redistributing load or inserting recovery windows—without the full cost of L1-L2 replanning.

experience_synthesis.insight: Under demand_surge, S2 was deterministically disqualified due to ergonomic and safety constraint violations (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80 dB); S3 cleared all hard constraints and satisfied the planner. The high deadline_gap_pct (60.6%) signals that even the accepted policy leaves substantial schedule slack unused, suggesting either the surge was partially absorbed or throughput headroom remains. Future planning should pre-screen policies for fatigue and noise compliance before evaluating throughput, and consider whether higher-throughput variants of S3 could close the deadline gap further. Confidence is very low given N=1; patterns may not generalise without additional trials.
